title: Q-PORT: Quantum Portfolio Optimization with Resource-Efficient Encoding and Scalability Analysis
journal_or_venue: Proceedings of the First International Conference, QUEST-IS 2025 (Communications in Computer and Information Science, CCIS 2743)
abstract_summary: This paper introduces Q-PORT, a systematic study of quantum portfolio optimization that evaluates the trade-offs between circuit depth, stock-to-qubit encoding strategies, and scalability for VQE- and QAOA-based methods. Through experiments on real market datasets and varying ansatz depths, the authors show that allocating multiple qubits per stock yields negligible gains over classical benchmarks, whereas encoding multiple stocks per qubit can substantially reduce resource requirements with only minor precision loss, enabling more scalable quantum portfolio optimization on NISQ-era devices. This study evaluates Iterative and Maximum Likelihood Quantum Amplitude Estimation (IAE and MLAE) for pricing European call options using historical Apple data, comparing quantum estimates against Black–Scholes and Monte Carlo benchmarks. Experiments on statevector simulators show both quantum methods return zero expected payoff due to coarse discretization from limited uncertainty qubits that fail to resolve low-probability, in-the-money tail events, highlighting the need for improved encoding and finer amplitude resolution despite algorithmic correctness in identifying realized outcomes.
methodology_description: Q-PORT evaluates quantum portfolio optimization by (1) collecting historical stock price data and computing classical Mean-Variance Optimization (MVO) as a baseline; (2) reformulating the portfolio optimization problem as a QUBO suitable for quantum algorithms; (3) experimenting with alternative encoding strategies (multi-qubit per stock and multi-stock-per-qubit compressed encodings) to study trade-offs between qubit resources and solution quality; (4) solving the QUBO with hybrid quantum-classical algorithms (VQE and QAOA) using layered parameterized ansätze and a classical optimizer (COBYLA); (5) systematically varying circuit depth (number of layers/repetitions) and encoding mappings; and (6) comparing quantum outputs to the classical MVO baseline over multiple stock sets (3, 4, and 12 tickers). The evaluation emphasizes scalability (how solution quality and resource needs change with problem size and encoding), the eﬀect of circuit repetitions, and practical constraints of NISQ-era hardware by running statevector simulations and measuring how often the quantum-generated portfolios align with the classical optimum.
experimental_setup: Statevector-based quantum simulators were used (noisy hardware was not used). All experiments were executed on Google Colab instances (Intel Xeon E5 CPUs). Circuits employed layered ansätze consisting of initial Hadamard layers, parameterized RZ rotations for the cost Hamiltonian, RZZ two-qubit entangling gates following the QUBO structure, and RX mixer gates. Circuit depth (number of repetitions/layers) was varied between 1 and 5. The classical optimizer COBYLA was used with a maximum of 5000 iterations. The risk tolerance was set to 0.2 and the investment budget was set to (number of stocks − 1).
dataset_used: Historical stock price data from Yahoo Finance covering January 1, 2020 to January 1, 2024. Three sets of assets were considered: (i) 3 stocks: Apple, Microsoft, Google; (ii) 4 stocks: Apple, Microsoft, Google, Amazon; (iii) 12 stocks: Apple, Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Tesla, Nvidia, Meta, Netflix, JP Morgan, Disney, Visa, Berkshire Hathaway. Expected returns and covariance matrices were derived from the historical prices and used to build classical MVO baselines and the QUBO formulation.

experiment_input.preprocessing: Classical computation of expected returns and the covariance matrix for each asset set. QUBO formulation derived from standard mean-variance objective plus budget/allocation constraints. For multi-stock-per-qubit encoding, a candidate pool of portfolios was generated and clustered with k-means prior to quantum evaluation.
experiment_input.dataset_size: varies by asset set; full historical time series for each asset over the 4-year period used to compute statistics (no per-circuit sample counts required for statevector simulation)

pipeline_steps: Collect historical prices and compute expected returns and covariance matrix (classical preprocessing).
Classically solve the MVO problem to obtain baseline optimal portfolios.
Formulate the portfolio optimization problem as a QUBO.
Select an encoding strategy: (a) multi-qubit per stock; (b) multi-stock-per-qubit (compressed) and for (b) generate candidate portfolios and cluster via k-means.
Construct parameterized quantum circuits for VQE or QAOA: initialize with Hadamard layers, apply RZ (cost), RZZ entanglers according to QUBO, and RX mixers.
Run the hybrid optimization with COBYLA (max iterations 5000), varying the number of layers (1–5) to study depth scaling.
Collect resulting candidate portfolios from quantum circuits, compute their classical performance (return/risk), and compare ranking/quality against the classical MVO solution.
Aggregate results across encodings, depths, and asset sets to evaluate scalability and resource/quality trade-offs.

results_summary: The Q-PORT paper introduces a systematic benchmarking methodology for quantum portfolio optimization that compares encoding strategies and circuit configurations using hybrid quantum-classical algorithms (VQE, QAOA) on statevector simulators. Empirical simulation results on 3-, 4-, and 12-stock problems indicate that allocating multiple qubits per stock provides negligible precision improvement over classical MVO in the tested regimes, while compressing several stocks into a single qubit considerably reduces resource demand with only small reductions in solution quality. The experiments varied circuit depth (1–5 layers) and ansatz choices and used MVO as the classical baseline. All experiments were run on ideal (noise-free) simulators, so conclusions about performance on NISQ hardware are tentative and require further noisy- or hardware-level validation. Two complementary empirical studies were reported. For portfolio optimization (Q-PORT), experiments on 3, 4 and 12-stock sets using VQE and QAOA in statevector simulation show that encoding multiple stocks per qubit can greatly reduce qubit counts while maintaining competitive solution rankings—especially for QAOA with deeper circuits—whereas assigning more qubits per stock (redundant encoding) generally increases search space complexity and often degrades performance unless depth is increased. For option pricing, QAE practical variants (IAE and MLAE) applied to real AAPL data with 6 uncertainty qubits failed to recover the positive expected payoff produced by classical Black–Scholes and Monte Carlo due to coarse discretization: both quantum estimators returned zero expected payoff while correctly predicting the realized (observed) payoff, highlighting encoding/resolution as the main bottleneck rather than the amplitude-estimation algorithms themselves.
performance_claims: Portfolio experiments: increasing circuit repetitions (layers 1→5) generally lowered the ranking (improved alignment) of the MVO-optimal solution for both QAOA and VQE; QAOA ranked the optimal solution among top positions at low depth for 3-stock cases (qualitative, no single numeric ranking provided).

contradictions: contradiction:classical-vs-quantum — The paper finds that straightforward multi-qubit-per-stock mappings deliver negligible gains over classical MVO, contradicting optimistic claims that naive quantum encodings will outperform classical baselines; instead, gains rely on careful compressed encodings and hybrid processing.
